column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article says he handed the Jesuits' Collège en Isle to his clergy as a seminary in 1786, two years after his death; left out. The article spells Velbrück with an umlaut; the entry writes Velbruck.
Thin article; the entry already gives the Rome and Siam journeys, the Académie and the Mémoires.

The entry says the paintings are now in the Villa Albani; the article says they were stored there from 1946 until the Italian state acquired them in 2026 and moved them to the Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia. Their present place is left out.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance (mostly a list of children); it also gives his birth as 1744 against the entry's 1745

The entry dates its transformation into the Provisional Government of the French Republic to June 1944; the article does not date that change but has the Allies recognising it as provisional government in September 1944. Neither date of the change is printed.
The article gives his second term as 54 days from 15 April and also says the crash came forty-five days after he took office; neither figure printed.
The article does not mention the United Suvadive Republic; not added.
Two sections only: the article is mostly a list of recordings; the entry already gives the dating, the Jistebnice hymnal and Piae Cantiones.

The article dates Soshangane's death to 1856 in its text but gives his reign as 1824-1858 and Mawewe's from 1858 in its list of monarchs; no year printed. The article also dates the empire's slave-trading to 1830-1897, beyond its end in 1895; years left out.

The article says the code was promulgated in 1792 (the first version, AGB) and 'finally codified in 1794'; the entry says it came into force in 1794. No year of the first version printed. The article gives over 17,000 articles; the entry about 19,000 paragraphs. No figure printed.

The entry calls the Seneca the westernmost nation of the Iroquois Confederacy and says the valley was their heartland; the article places them between the Genesee and Canandaigua Lake. Not printed either way beyond the gorge as a border. The Seneca's move to reclaim Canawaugus in December 2022 left out as a present-day claim.
The article says he was born at Kiplin in late 1579 while dating him 1580; no year of birth printed.

The entry says he failed at Bharatpur after four assaults; the article says it held out against five. No number printed. The article has Lake arriving at Castlebar on 29 August and witnessing the rout, without a separate date for the battle; written as late in August.
The article's lead dates his attempted return to May 1865, its body to June 1865; no month printed. Birth date disputed in the article (24 September or 3 October 1813); left out.

The article dates his assumption of the royal title to 19 October 1818 (and his coins to AH 1234, 1818); the entry says 1819. No year printed. The article says he appointed George Duncan Beechey after Home's retirement in 1828, after his own death; left out. The article says his coins replaced the name of Shah Alam II; left out as doubtful (the name is the article's).
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; adds only the source, tributaries and two early mentions (Sarsa Dengel 1566, António Fernandes 1613)
The entry gives 1079 and Sky Hill for his seizure of Mann; the article excerpt dates it only 'within the decade' of the 1070s and does not name Sky Hill. Neither added nor contradicted.
The article gives 27 or 24 towers; I wrote 27 as its main figure.
The article speaks of the submission of Nagabhata II, where the entry says he was defeated; worded as submission without contradicting the entry.
The article does not mention the Qing Grand Council or the date 1729 given in the entry; nothing about it was written.
The article says Barrow had replaced Adams as Premier by 1961, though Adams had left the premiership for the federation in 1958; worded as Barrow being Premier by 1961.
The article dates the reduction to 1680; the entry says the 1680s. No year was given for its start in the text.
The article does not mention the referendum named in the entry; it gives 1 December 1946 for the establishment of Hesse and the first elections.

The article calls the three brothers kings of a triumvirate reigning about three years; the entry calls Gulussa a prince and says he died before Micipsa. Worded as shared royal power, with no title or length of reign.

The article contradicts itself and the entry on the reign. Its lead gives c. 970-989; its foundation section argues for proclamation in 981 (Mkhitar Ayrivanetsi), cites a 979 memorandum calling him only prince of Tashir, and says Smbat II formally recognised him as king in 982. The entry says he took the title around 979. These dates were left out; only the dispute (966-988 proposed) and the 986 khachkar were given. The article also says Gagik I (990-1020) confirmed Gurgen on his throne, which conflicts with the entry's end of reign in 989 and with the article's own account of his death in 989; left out. The Haghpat church is said to be completed during his reign in one section and in 991 in another; no completion date given.
SKIPPED: article has about 200 words of substance beyond a family list, and most of it is already in the description

The article's legacy section quotes Kalhana's Rajatarangini as praising her, which cannot be (Kalhana wrote in the 12th century); left out. The article dates Yusuf's loss of the throne to 1580 and his recovery to 1581, and the annexation to 1586; the entry's 'exile after the Mughal conquest of 1586' was not restated.

The article is mostly a family list and says nothing of the rebellion of 1746 or the Treaty of Giyanti beyond naming it; the text keeps to family and succession. Paragraph 'In 1758 Raden Mas Sundoro...' is short; may be merged.

The article mentions a gravestone in Mecca for a Shaykh Hamza b. Abd Allah al-Fansuri dated 11 April 1527, whose identification is challenged; if correct, Hamzah would not have worked in Aceh, against the entry's 'active in Aceh in the late 16th century'. Left out, as was the article's dating of his hajj to the early 16th century.

The article names the chancellor Qin Hui; the entry writes Qin Gui. The chancellor is left unnamed in the text so the page does not show two forms of the name. The Huangtiandang section of the article is empty in the saved copy; the battle is in the entry and was not retold. Left out the article's claim that Han led Song Jiang's army against the Liao (a Water Margin story) and the reported speeches of his outburst at court.

The entry dates the move of the capital to the late 12th century; the article says only 'during the reign of Ganapati Deva', with no date; no date given in the text. The article says the Thousand Pillar Temple was 'destroyed' by Muslim invaders, though it stands today; written as 'damaged'.
SKIPPED: article is a genealogy: about 150 words of substance beyond lists of children and ancestors, most of it already in the description
The entry's purple robes are not in the article; nothing about dress was written.
The article dates the industrial growth of the Hellweg towns 'from the Early Modern period'; written without a period.

The article gives his dates as c. 850 to after May 912 and says he lived in the 9th and 10th centuries; the entry's dates read '9th century'. The year of his last appearance (May 912) was left out of the text. The article spells the son Gutier and Gutierre Menéndez; Gutierre used.
The article is short (about 480 words) and the entry already gives most of its History section; this text adds the etymology, the hirdman title, the gestir and the council rank. Two sections only.

The article calls Leo IX the uncle of Count Adalbert, hence 'his nephew'. The article places Duke Christoph's school after the end of the community, in a paragraph that follows 1648, although Christoph lived in the 16th century; the text gives no date for the school.

The article also calls the laws the Code of the Nesilim; not used. The entry speaks of compensation; the article says the usual penalty for serious offences was enslavement to forced labour. Both are kept compatible: the text speaks only of serious offences.
The article does not date Ulrich's elevation (the entry gives 1464); the text gives no year.
The article is mostly about the present organisation; the history of the House (1867, 1881) is in the entry and not in the article's text given.
Living members (the 14th Prince and his heirs) are left out. The entry's statement that a branch took the Arenberg name is not in the article, which lists Arenberg only among the cadet branches.

The article gives the Catholic line's princely rank as 1711 in the text and 1712 in its list of rulers; the text says 'early in the 18th century'. The article says Henry sold Löwenstein to Frederick I, Count Palatine, in 1441; the text names only the Palatine branch of the Wittelsbachs. The article's lead says the house ruled from 1488, its text 1494; only 1494 (Louis made a count) is used. The entry names Clara Tott as Louis's mother; the article does not name her, and the text does not.

The entry says the palace was the first building in East Africa to have electricity and a lift; the article says the first in Zanzibar to have electricity and the first in East Africa to have a lift. Neither is repeated. The entry says the palace was damaged in 1896; the article says it suffered only minor damage. The text does not describe its own damage.

The article includes a very small portion of Guanajuato, which the entry does not list; the text mentions it without contradicting the entry's list. The entry's statement on tribute to the Aztec Empire is not in the article; not repeated. The article's economy section (poverty, 'critical region') and transport (as of June 2026) left out.

The entry says the 1851 climb was the first recorded ascent of the summit plateau; the article calls it the first documented ascent of Mount Kinabalu. The text gives only the dates of his visits. The article says he was colonial secretary 1848–1850 and police magistrate 1850–1877; the entry says he served in Labuan from 1848.

The article gives Dominica's hit at 150 mph (Category 4) and the Category 5 peak later; the entry calls it a Category 5 hurricane that struck Dominica. The text gives no category or wind speed for Dominica.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, most of it already in the entry; it also dates the second sack to 341, where the entry has 342
The quotation is from the translation the article gives (from Wikisource).

The article does not date the revolt (the entry gives 1144) or name Mértola; the text follows the entry's account without dates. The Portuguese king is not named in the text: the article spells him 'Alfonso Henrique', the entry 'Afonso Henriques'.
The article is short; two sections. Asad Khan Lari is said to be buried in Belgaum (not used).
The article dates Shaw's work only to 1959; the entry gives 1959–64. The text gives no year for it. The 2013 vigilante violence is left out.

The article's dating of his early service is muddled ('In 1579, during the Siege of Itami (1574)'); only the 1580 siege is used. It says both that he took part in the Korean invasions and that he stayed in Japan guarding the east; the text follows the detail.

The entry says it was at first a reserve force; the article says it consisted of regular units and was fully established with regular troops, without describing an earlier reserve stage. The text does not describe its status before 1914.
The article also quotes a military historian on Shaka's assassination in 1828; not used.
The article gives Joaquim Silvério dos Reis the dates 1756–1792, the same as Freire de Andrade's; not used.

The entry says Indo-Fijians outnumbered indigenous Fijians by the 1940s; the article gives a majority of about 52% only for the late 20th century. The text gives no decade for when they became the larger group.
The article's legacy section says the Khmer Rouge genocide took place during the Cambodian Civil War (1970-1975) and that the CPP was replaced by the Khmer Rouge; this looks garbled and was left out.
The article dates his death to 53 BC; the entry gives d. 54/53 BCE. The text gives no year for his death.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: location, the kallanka's size, a few structures, a UNESCO tentative listing and an opera; too little beyond the entry
The article dates the Abu Salabikh copies to the early and to the mid third millennium BCE in different places; the entry gives c. 2600-2500 BCE. The text gives no date.
The entry names the Sulu Sultanate as the Iranun's ally; the article names only the Maguindanao Sultanate, under whose flag they fought. The text mentions Maguindanao only.
The article calls him ruler from 1869 until his death, a reign of 63 years; the entry has him ruler until 1923, keeping the title until death. The text says he held the title for 63 years.

The entry says the 1189 marriage brought Marshal the earldom of Pembroke; the article says the earldom was revived for him in 1199. The text gives 1199 without saying the entry is wrong, as the claim came through the marriage.
The entry says the 25th Army reached Pyongyang within days; the article says it relocated to the Pyongyang area in late August. The text gives no timing.
The article does not mention the Kabylia campaign of 1857 or Fort-Napoléon named in the entry; the text leaves them to the entry.
The article calls Man Singh I his grandfather in one place but makes his predecessor Bhau Singh, a younger son of Man Singh, his grand-uncle; the text names Man Singh I without a relationship.

The article dates his succession as earl to 24 February 1633 but its lead says Earl of Ormond from 1634, and it gives the start of the English Civil War as both August and September 1642; the text gives neither date.

The entry says the Cape was taken from the Dutch East India Company with Admiral Elphinstone's fleet; the article says from the Dutch Republic, naming Vice-Admiral Viscount Keith. The text names neither the former holder nor the admiral.
The article dates his East Indies command from January 1854 in one place and his flag hoisted on 11 May 1854 in another; the text gives neither.

The article gives his death as 23 November 1694 in the lead and 24 November 1694 in its Legacy section; only the year is given here. The article says he became intendant 'when he was 30', which does not fit a commission of 1665 for a man born in 1626; left out. Seigneury grants (about sixty between 10 October and 8 November, 31 on 3 November) are given without a year in the article, so the dates were not printed.

The article says he spent seventeen years as an Oirat slave (1716-1733); the entry says nearly twenty years among the Dzungars. The length of the captivity is not stated here. The article does not say when or where he died; the heading is Legacy for that reason.
The article mentions a 'second war' with the Basotho but does not give its start date; only its treaty is dated here.
Death: the entry says 'possibly in 1150'; the article adds 'or in early 1151 at the latest', which is kept as the article words it and does not contradict the entry's c. 1150.

The article says Okello was 'baptized at age two, receiving the baptismal name of Gideon'; kept to the baptism only. His death is unknown (vanished after 1971; murder by Amin believed by most observers according to Petterson); the heading Death and legacy covers the disappearance.

The entry dates his conversion to Catholicism to 1612; the article gives 25 December 1613. The year is left out here. The article spells the son both Johan Frans Desideratus and John Francis Desideratus; the English form is used.
The article is short (about 350 words); the text keeps to its facts. The article does not say how he came to be called Rajačić-Brinski beyond the name itself.

The article places Quiroga's final defeat of Lamadrid 'in Salta'; the entry names the battle La Ciudadela (which other sources place at Tucumán). The place is left out here. The article's claim of descent from the Visigothic king Reccared I was left out as a family tradition the article does not source.

The entry says he was arrested and shot by German troops in April 1918. The article gives his death as 2 May 1918, at Hauho near Hämeenlinna (place unconfirmed), and says that according to the official version he was executed by German troops in Helsinki, while recent research suggests a unit of the Swedish Brigade may have killed him at Hauho. The date, place and killers are left out here. Heading Legacy, as the circumstances of the death are disputed and not told.

SKIPPED: Article too thin: under 150 words of history (Wu Wen-ji's collection, his renaming at a Kuomintang academy, Yu Yixuan's performance), the rest a list of covers and samples in films and video games.

The article gives his death as 20 June 1277, 1278 or 30 May 1279; the entry says 1278. No year is given here. The article dates the language decree to 13 May 1277 in the lead and the firman section, but tells it as issued at the council after Siyavush's enthronement on 15 May. The decree is left undated here.

The article gives the start of the Michigan excavations as both 1924 ('Beginning in 1924') and 1925 ('received grants ... in 1924. Starting excavations of Karanis in 1925'); the entry says from 1924. The year is left out here. The article dates the papyri both to the Diocletian-370s period and calls the latest papyrus early fifth century; the date range of the papyri is not given here.

The entry dates his death c. 1365; the article says he died between 1358 and 1363, most likely in or before 1362, from the undated division of Navahrudak between Vaidotas and Tautvilas and Vaidotas's capture at Kaunas in 1362. That reasoning is left out; only the 1358 and 1366 mentions are given. The article says Fedir inherited Navahrudak from his father but also that Navahrudak was divided between the sons of Kęstutis; Fedir's Navahrudak inheritance is left out.

The article also gives Seshadri Sastri's dating of 113-135 CE; left out to keep the dating paragraph short, and both fit the entry's early centuries CE. Much of the article rests on Sangam poems and medieval inscriptions and claims; the conquests of Ceylon, Andhra and the north are given as the traditions' and poems' accounts. The article's paragraph on 12,000 Sinhalese men taken as slaves is tied to the reign of Vankanasika Tissa without a clear source; left out.

SKIPPED: Article too thin: under 250 words, mostly modern geography (bridge, pylons, newspaper); its few historical lines (Grímnismál, Haraldshaugen, Magnus Olsen on the name Norway) add little to the entry.

The entry says the castle was built around 1254 by Geoffrey of Bruyères; the article says only 'mid-13th century', which agrees. The article's 1320 date for the Byzantine capture is the entry's too; not repeated.

The article says in its lead that commercial production began in September 2013, and later that commercial output started in November 2016; the entry says production was delayed until 2016. The text says only that oil first flowed in 2013 before the leak, and dates the first export. Cost estimates (US$116 billion per CNN Money in 2012, other sources up to $50 billion) and the 'largest discovery in 30 years' ranking were left out.

The article dates the Elamite sack to 1160 BCE and the dynasty's end to 1155 BCE; the entry says around 1158 BCE. The fall is left out (the entry tells it). The article gives the dynasty's span as 1595-1155 BCE and the king list's 576 years, adding that it probably ruled around 350 years; left out against the entry's 'about four centuries'.
The article calls the Mwata's title Mwata Yav in its lead, which seems to confuse the Kazembe title with that of the western Lunda king; not used.
The article calls both Hiriya Venkatappa Nayaka and Shivappa Nayaka the greatest ruler of the dynasty; neither judgement printed.
The article has little history; the Tanjungpura and Matan kingdoms of the entry are mentioned only through the royal cemetery.

The article dates Khalaf's surrender to December 1002 and gives his reign as 963-1002; the entry says he surrendered in 1003. The year is left out. The article says Khalaf lived in Guzgan until 1006 or 1007; not printed.

Rowland dates the art of Khalchayan to the end of the 2nd century BCE, while the article elsewhere dates the decoration to the mid-1st century BCE (the entry: around the 1st century BCE). Rowland's date is not printed.

The entry says Khusrau Shah ruled from Lahore after Ghazni was lost to Oghuz Turkmen; the article does not mention Lahore or the Oghuz and implies he was at Ghazni. Nothing on his seat is printed. Short article; the text is close to its limit.
Population figure (approximately 7,657) not printed; the SIGINT station and Nabi Tajima left out.

The article also gives, from another source, a reign of 378-343 BCE; not printed, as it does not fit the entry's death in 320 BCE. The article does not mention Guiling, Zou Ji or the meeting at Xuzhou in 334 BCE.

The article does not mention the revolt of 1633, Tlemcen or the exclusion from the janissary corps given in the entry. Much of the article's Legacy section concerns Ottoman influence in general (music, Karagöz); left out.

The entry says he ruled from Sarai; the article says that although master of Sarai he remained based primarily on Astrakhan. His seat is left out. The descendants' list is flat in the saved text, so grandsons are not named individually.

The article gives the UNESCO listing as 2012 in one place and calls it the 2011 entry in another; the entry says 2011. The year is left out. The article says the manuscripts were written down between the 18th and 20th century; the entry says mostly of the 18th and 19th. Only the earliest date is given.
The article calls her one of the most influential leaders in Eswatini's history; not printed as a judgement.

The article dates the reign to c. 724-760 (modern historians), while the entry says the first half of the 8th century; no reign dates printed. The article calls the Martand Sun Temple now destroyed; the entry says its ruins still stand. The temple is left out.

The article says the inhabitants at first did not have Roman citizenship after the conquest of 338 BCE and acquired it later; the entry says they received it after the Latin War in 338 BCE. Citizenship is left out.

The entry says he was succeeded by Petru I Mușat; the article says some sources have Lațcu deposing his nephew Petru I in 1368, and that the Vlachs elected George Koriatovich after his death. The succession is left out. The article dates his death to around 1374 or 1375; the entry says c. 1375. No year printed.

The article's lead says over 60% of the convicted were released in 1936, while its own figures give 37,425 of more than 91,000; the percentage is left out. The comparison with Russian court figures of 2017 is left out.

The article's lead says he was emperor 'from 1453' (the formal handover of power at 12); the entry says 1442 to 1459. I describe 1453 only as the formal handing of power, which fits the entry. The article says his mother 'remained in control of the government until the 1459 coup'; the entry says she governed as regent until 1453. Left that point out. Death date: the lead gives 25 October 1459, the body says the plotters struck on October 28. Neither printed.
SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance beyond the printed lyrics

Two sections only: the article has nothing on the place today. The article ends the voivodeship with 'the partitions of Poland in 1772–1795'; the entry says the Second Partition of 1793. I did not print the end. Area: the article gives 4,080 km2, Gloger '80 square miles' (old Polish miles), and the three counties add up to 4,376 km2. I printed only 4,080.
'affranchisement' rendered as 'the freeing of the unfree'.

The entry says the law 'required an interval between offices'. The article attributes this to Evans as a likelihood (an 'obligatory biennium ... at least between praetorship and consulship'), and Mommsen treats the biennium as an existing principle. I left the interval out rather than hedge against the entry.
The excerpt does not say how he came into Xu Wen's household or how Xu Zhixun's challenge ended; left out. The article does not give the date of Xu Wen's death in the excerpt; not printed.

The official histories say Li Shimin persuaded Li Yuan to rebel; Wen Daya's Da Tang Chuangye Qijuzhu credits Li Yuan himself. Not printed. The banquet at the Eastern Palace at which Li Shimin fell ill is disputed in date and truth; left out. The article names a brother Li Zhiyun who died on the journey, though its own list of Duchess Dou's sons omits him; left out.

Birth year: the article's lead gives 5 November 1885 (as the entry), its Early life section 1886. I gave no year of birth. The article says Li launched the Fujian revolt with Chen Mingshu; the entry speaks of the leaders of the 19th Route Army. I named neither, mentioning only the revolt's defeat.

The article follows the traditional account that Li Shimin persuaded Li Yuan to rebel; the article on Li Jiancheng says another source credits Li Yuan himself. Left the question out. Duchess Dou's death: this article says 614, the Li Jiancheng article only 'before Tang's establishment'. Not printed.

The article dates the Austrian entry to 12 January 1791 in one place and the prince-bishop's return to 12 February 1791 in another; I gave no date for the restoration (the entry says January 1791). The vote figures for the city are those given: 9,700 registered, 40 no, 748 conditional, 1,548 outright, the rest for a merger with some conditions.
Left out the 2019 solar-power scheme and the planned dam on Hadakiya Creek (a plan, not a lasting fact).
SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance (mostly a family list) and adds little to the description; it also dates the fall of the Later Han to 950, the entry to 951

The entry says he fought Macedon 'in the 230s BCE'; the article dates his victory over Demetrius II to 229 BCE. I gave 231 for Bylazora and no year for the victory. The article gives his reign as c. 231 to 206 BCE.

The article says he 'authored' the Bayonet Constitution; the entry says he 'helped force' it. My wording ('the constitution he wrote was imposed') is consistent with both. The article says the overthrow was 'supported by the U.S. Military' and that Congress apologised for the involvement of the Marine Corps.

The article says he was assassinated by William de la Marck; the entry says by followers of William de la Marck. I wrote 'in the attack of William de la Marck', which fits both. The article says Marc de Bade was put in place by the Liégeois, 'who fought under Raes van Heers, restored the bishop, but Liège lost its sovereignty': a garbled sentence, left out. 'Reign' used for a prince-bishop as ruler of the principality.
The article writes 'Louis I (d 1140)' as the son of Louis the Springer who married Hedwig; I wrote 'His son Louis ... made him landgrave' without the numeral to keep the sentence simple.

SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance (mostly transliterated inscriptions); it also dates him to the end of the 25th century BCE and has him claim kingship of Kish, where the entry says the 24th century and Uruk and Ur
SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance and adds little to the description

The article dates the Nine Armies' War to 1785 and the Tha Din Daeng campaign to 1786; the entry gives the war as 1785–1786. I gave only 1785 for the invasion and 1786 for the campaigns, which fits both. The article's own date for the Vientiane campaign is 1778–1779; the entry says capture in 1779. Not dated in my text.

The article dates the conquest of Mrauk U to 1784 under Crown Prince Thado Minsaw (and the bronzes' removal to 1785); the entry says 1785 under Bodawpaya. The year of the conquest is left out. The article names the legendary king Candrasurya and Sanda Thuriya; the entry has Chandrasuriya.
The article says the poem was completed when Nizami was forty years old; with his birth in 1141 that gives about 1181, which contradicts its own date of 1165-1173. The age is left out.
SKIPPED: the article has well under 250 words of substance (source, course, tributaries, one dam) and adds little to the description
The article says Sambanthan served as president until 1971 but also that he was forced to retire in favour of Manickavasagam in 1973; his end year is left out.

The article says the Mamprusi began converting to Islam in the 17th century; the entry says Islam spread among them from the 18th century. The century is left out. The article spells the founder both Naa Gbewaa and Naa Gbanwaah; Gbewaa is used.

The article gives his death as 20 December 1940 in the lead and 19 December 1940 in the Death section; the day is left out. The entry says he fled to Angola after the rising failed; the article says he was taken to German South-West Africa after being wounded. Neither is stated.
The article gives his birth as 1319; the entry has c. 1317. The birth year is left out.

The article says crusade proposals circulated in the early thirteenth century, evidently a slip for the fourteenth; left out. The article names his patron both Cardinal Riccardo Petroni and Riccardo of Siena; the patron is not named in the motive sentence.
The article says he became clan leader in 445 BCE in its lead but that his father died in 446 BCE in the body; the year of succession is left out (the entry gives r. 445).
The article dates the dedication of the kingdom to Padmanabha both to January 1750 and to 1749-50; the entry's 1750 is not repeated.
Kiesewetter suggests Matthew became master of the islands only about 1206; the entry says he held them by about 1195. The later date is left out.

The article says the province's position and capital remain uncertain, with London and the south-east only the usual modern view, based on the governor's consular rank; the entry states the capital as Londinium. The uncertainty is not stated in the text.
The article dates the Gesta to after 1150; the entry says around 1200. No date for the Gesta is given in the text.
The article says he was sole ruler from 1273 (the civil war lasting until 1273, Gdańsk recovered in 1273); the entry says he ruled the whole of Gdańsk Pomerania from 1271. The year is left out.

The article dates his appointment as Sar-i-Khail both 'between February 1634 and December 1636' and 23 June 1637; written as 'in the 1630s'. The article gives his arrival in Golconda as 1630, with 1615 or 1620 suggested by some scholars; kept with that hedge. Left out the article's praise of his 'magnificent leadership' and the exaggerated booty figures.
The entry lists Slavic tribes (Drougoubitai, Strymonians, Belegezites); the article does not name them, so they are not repeated.

The article gives the restoration's completion as June 2018 (and 20 June 2018 for the 'second restoration'), and the start of dismantling as 1999; the entry says the pagoda was restored between 2001 and 2019. Both versions left out. The article calls the pagoda both 'among the oldest' and 'the oldest' of Korean pagodas; not repeated.
The entry dates the ruling to December 1891; the article gives no date for the fatwa, only the telegram of 26 July 1891. Left out the present-day family link to Ali al-Sistani (a living person).
The article dates the start of construction to 900-955 or 900-950 CE; the entry says built from about 950. The start date is left out.
The article names Yergin and Stanislaw by surname only.
The article is short; the text uses nearly all of it, including the decree's articles.
The entry says King You was killed there 'according to tradition'; the article states it as fact. Written without the hedge in the article's terms but without contradicting the entry's account.

The entry says the crusaders of 1344 held the harbour castle; the article says the port was held by the Genoese until Tamerlane took it in 1403. Who held the port is left unnamed. The entry credits the refoundation to Antigonus and Lysimachus around 300 BCE; the article names only Lysimachos for the walls and ties the move to Alexander. Only the walls of Lysimachos and the legend are given.
Garanganze oral history gives other versions of the killing (Msiri spearing Bodson); only the expedition's version, which the entry follows, is told, with the shooter named.
